author: Ko Ju-Chun (葛如鈞)
text: The Agent-Building Agent Era Just Started — Sierra's Ghostwriter (Bret Taylor) ships the first production agent that BUILDS other agents: upload SOPs, call transcripts, whiteboard photos, or describe in English. Ghostwriter identifies agent type, deploys config, writes system prompt, creates tools + knowledge base, sets escalation paths. Zero eng required.
suggestedEngagement: The 'zero eng required' framing raises the governance wall fast — when an AI-built agent takes an action the original spec author never anticipated, who owns the blast radius? Ask if Ghostwriter enforces least-privilege defaults on generated agents.
The real question is whether Ghostwriter produces verifiable agent specs or just a prompt+tools blob — that distinction determines whether you can audit what was deployed.
This is the agent-harness-as-IDE moment. The architecture of what it outputs (encodable safety properties vs. free-form prompts) is the durable enterprise differentiation question.

author: Ko Ju-Chun (葛如鈞)
text: The Reliability Gap is the real bottleneck for AI agents — not capability. Princeton benchmarked frontier models across 14 reliability metrics: Claude Opus 4.5 + Gemini 3 Pro at 85% overall reliability, but Gemini scored only 25% on SAFETY metrics. A model that's 85% reliable but 25% safe isn't enterprise-ready — it's a liability.
suggestedEngagement: 25% safety score with 85% capability is exactly the gap that stalls enterprise procurement — reliability and safety aren't the same metric. Is the Princeton benchmark reproducible across deployment contexts?
The real risk is that teams measuring 'reliability' aren't measuring safety failure modes at all — they're measuring task completion rate. Ask which of the 14 metrics showed widest variance.
This quantifies the harness/guardrail leverage opportunity: where the model is systematically weak is where the orchestration layer can compensate.
